name: US deep-sea freight services, producer price index (BLS)
note: Producer price index: not a freight rate. 1988 to 2026: values retrieved through FRED, the St. Louis Fed's copy of this BLS series, until the BLS API answers for these years; the latest months may be preliminary
basis: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, producer price index by industry, deep sea freight transportation (NAICS 483111), series PCU483111483111, not seasonally adjusted, June 1988 = 100. It measures the change in the prices US-based deep-sea carriers receive for their freight services. It is not a spot freight rate and moves far less than the Baltic indices: +0.7% from May to December 2008 (256.5 to 258.2) while dry bulk rates collapsed, then a fall of 27% from September 2008 (284.4) to May 2009 (208.8).

name: Global Supply Chain Pressure Index (New York Fed)
note: Supply-chain pressure, partly built on freight indices: not a freight rate
basis: Federal Reserve Bank of New York: the index combines transport costs (the Baltic Dry Index, the Harpex container index and the BLS air freight cost indices) with supply-chain components of manufacturing PMI surveys in seven economies; readings are standard deviations from the index's historical average, and the last months are revised as data come in. Cite as: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Global Supply Chain Pressure Index, https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/policy/gscpi. The GSCPI is not an official estimate of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, its President, the Federal Reserve System, or the Federal Open Market Committee.

name: Index of global real economic activity (Dallas Fed, Kilian)
note: Deflated, detrended index built on dry bulk freight rates: not a freight rate
basis: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas: “Updated index of global real economic activity in industrial commodity markets, as proposed in Kilian (2009), with the correction discussed in Kilian (2019). This business-cycle index is expressed in percent deviations from trend. It is derived from a panel of dollar-denominated global bulk dry cargo shipping rates and may be viewed as a proxy for the volume of shipping in global industrial commodity markets.” Kilian, L. (2009), American Economic Review 99(3), doi:10.1257/aer.99.3.1053; Kilian, L. (2019), Economics Letters 178, doi:10.1016/j.econlet.2019.03.001.
